extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, editors, and content creators interested in the craft and use of single-panel cartoons
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing effective single-panel cartoons—how to craft a complete joke or commentary in one frame using composition, captioning, visual suggestion, and iterative refinement; also covers uses and stylistic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy / Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: One image. One caption (if that). The single-panel cartoon relies on economy—there's no room for fluff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires the reader to make a cognitive leap, spot the visual gag, and understand context quickly. The form's power comes from saying something in a very small space; aim for concise, concentrated delivery rather than extended setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained completeness (one-frame punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single-panel cartoon tells a complete story or delivers a punchline in one frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike comic strips with multiple panels and time progression, the single-panel must communicate its situation and payoff immediately. Ensure the image+caption work together to form a full, interpretable idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose every element with precision: composition is essential in a tight space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every visual element must earn its place; deliberate placement directs attention to the joke or point. Composition choices determine pacing, focus, and the reader's path through the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character expression and posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Use expression and body language (a raised eyebrow, posture) to suggest meaning and subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small changes in a character's posture or expression can change the joke's interpretation; cartoonists often tweak these details across drafts to refine the gag or tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption wording and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Caption wording and the rhythm of the line are crucial to timing and punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoonists sketch multiple versions and adjust caption phrasing and cadence to find the funniest or most effective delivery. Word choice (including double-meaning words) can supply the punchline or ambiguity needed for the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of negative space
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative space is a compositional tool to focus attention and shape timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically leave space to isolate elements, emphasize the gag, or create visual pauses. In a single frame, silence/space functions like a beat in comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual suggestion, implication, and irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on implication, irony, and visual shorthand rather than explicit exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small visual cues (objects, placement, props) carry meaning; the form depends on the reader inferring details rather than spelling everything out. Use irony and juxtaposition to create a layered or surprising punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative refinement and sketching
rubrics_metrics.description: The best single-panel cartoons may feel effortless but are refined through multiple sketches and tweaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch multiple versions of a joke, tweak posture, caption rhythm, and composition. Avoid accepting the first draft; refinement finds the most economical and surprising expression of the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimalist visual style and caption preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-panel art tends to be more minimal and often eschews speech bubbles in favor of captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a dialogue between image and text rather than within the frame; a minimalist approach directs focus to the visual wit and timing rather than dense drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation for editorial/commentary impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-panel cartoons can distill complex political or social issues into a single unforgettable image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for commentary (rather than pure gag), focus on a single pointed metaphor or symbolic image that captures the issue—examples include Herblock's anti-McCarthy cartoons or New Yorker pieces skewering Wall Street.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of intent: gag vs. commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the cartoon's goal is to amuse, provoke, educate, or combine those aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all single-panels aim for laughs; aligning tone, iconography, and caption with your intent ensures the reader interprets the piece as intended (e.g., satire vs. light gag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability to modern platforms and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-panel cartoons are well suited to digital sharing and a variety of practical uses (newsletters, social media, presentations, e-learning, greeting cards, merch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider platform norms (image size, cropping, audience attention span) when composing and captioning. The format's shareability can amplify impact but may require adjustments for different media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct personal voice / recognizable style
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the compact form, personal voice and stylistic signature should still shine through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a consistent visual and comedic voice (line quality, recurring motifs, tonal preferences) so work becomes instantly recognizable, as with notable cartoonists cited on the page.
